Short‐chain acyl‐PTMs play a vital role in cancer progression by regulating protein stability, enzyme activity, and protein nuclear localization

Short‐chain acyl‐PTMs play a vital role in cancer progression by regulating protein stability, enzyme activity, and protein nuclear localization. (A) Short‐chain acyl‐PTMs can affect the stability of essential proteins involved in tumor progression. Lactylation inhibits protein degradation processes, while succinylation and 2‐hydroxyisobutyrylation exert dual effects on protein stability, either stabilizing or promoting degradation. (B) Short‐chain acyl‐PTMs regulate the enzyme activity through addition of acyl groups (such as succinyl, crotonyl, and lactyl) to key sites in the enzymatic activity center to increase or reduce enzyme activity. (C) Short‐chain acyl‐PTMs, including succinylation, crotonylation, malonylation, and lactylation, can facilitate the nuclear localization of proteins, thereby promoting tumor initiation and progression. The modified proteins, modification sites, and induced biological effects have been shown in the same color font. PTMs labeled with dotted lines indicate the removal of the modification. The “OFF” in red font refers decrease of protein degradation or enzyme activity following acylation modification, while the “ON” in red font refers increase of protein degradation or enzyme activity.
